articles.title: Automatic computational reproducibility checks with Metacheck
articles.content:
When authors share their data and analysis code, the idea is that anyone should be able to run that code on that data and get the results reported in the paper. But sharing data and code in a way that results are reproducible is difficult, and researchers have often not received training in how to share data and code. As a consequence, there are often basic mistakes in public repositories that stand in the way of computationally reproducible results. Automated checks can help researchers identify and fix these mistakes, such as not sharing all files that are loaded in code, using absolute instead of relative file-paths, using values that are not computed in the code that is shared, changing file names so they no longer match the code, or not loading all libraries.

Checking whether data and code is reproducible is tedious. It also often requires repeated back and forths between the person performing the checks, and the researchers sharing data and code. Ideally, checks do not just focus on whether code runs, but also whether all results in a manuscript are reproduced by the code, but this takes a lot of time.

Metacheck’s reproducibility_check module attempts to perform all these checks automatically. When it succeeds, researchers and/or reviewers, data managers, or editors know that data and code is shared in a reproducible manner, and they do not need to perform manual checks. This saves everyone time, and leads to data and code repositories that are more useful for science. Our reproducibility check module is completely code-based. It uses no AI (although modules it builds on, such as data_check, can optionally use a large language model, by setting llm_use(TRUE), to better understand the files in a repository, such as which files belong to which study), and it can run locally on your computer without sending information to an external server.


If I say so myself, it is pretty damn cool. It is one of the rare experiences where I honestly thought something could not be done, but where I surprised myself because it actually works.

This post shows the module at work on two versions of the same small study: one where every reported result can be reproduced, and one where several cannot.

Computationally reproducing a simple Stroop experiment

Both papers analyse the same classroom data from my introduction to psychology and technology course. Students named the ink color of words that matched the color (the word “red” printed in red) and of words that did not (the word “red” printed in green), and reported the time they needed in seconds. Both papers report four results: the mean and standard deviation of the reaction times in each condition, the correlation between the reaction times in the two conditions, a paired t-test for the Stroop effect, and a comparison of the Stroop effect between the students tested in 2013 and in 2014.

  • The good paper, https://github.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper, computes every reported number in its analysis code. The manuscript is a Quarto document, so the text prints these numbers directly from the analysis.
  • The bad paper, https://github.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad, has several common mistakes deliberately built in. The results were typed into the text by hand, the shared data contain a value the authors removed before their own analysis without saying so, some reported results are not computed by the code at all, and the code stops with an error before it reaches the last analysis.

Running the code locally, or using our server on SURF

The reproducibility check runs code that other people wrote. That is not without risk. A script can delete files, read files that have nothing to do with the project, or send information over the internet, by accident or on purpose. By default, execute = TRUE runs each script in a separate R process on your own computer. This prevents a script that crashes from taking your own R session down with it, but the script can still reach every file on your computer, and the internet. That is fine for the two repositories in this post, which I wrote myself, but not for code from a repository you have not created, as a bad actor might insert problematic code.

For such code, add sandbox = "docker". Docker is a program that runs software in a container: a closed environment on your computer, separated from the rest of the system. Metacheck runs every script in its own container, and has set up these containers so that the code can do as little harm as possible:

  • The container has no internet connection while the code runs. Only the step before it, which installs the packages the code needs, is connected to the internet, and in that step none of the paper’s own code runs.
  • The code runs on a copy of the repository’s files, in a temporary folder. That folder is the only place on your computer it can write to, and the files on the rest of your computer are not visible inside the container.
  • The code runs as an ordinary user without administrator rights, cannot obtain extra rights, and can start only a limited number of processes.
  • Each script is stopped after a time limit, 10 minutes by default.

No sandbox makes running unknown code completely safe: a flaw in Docker itself could in principle still be exploited. But these settings close off the usual ways in which a script can do damage. The Reproducibility Check chapter lists the exact settings, and compares them with running code without Docker.

Running the check in Docker takes some preparation, and disk space. You need Docker Desktop (on Windows and macOS) or Docker Engine (on Linux), and the space Docker Desktop itself needs. The first time you run the check, Docker downloads Metacheck’s image for R code: R, Quarto, and the roughly 750 R packages that occurred in a scan of thousands of R files shared with psychology papers, together about 4.9 GB. Python code runs in a second image of about 2.7 GB. Because most packages a paper needs are already in the image, they do not have to be installed again for every paper, which makes the check much faster (but at the expense of a large docker image that you install once). The chapter explains how the image was built.

If you do not use R, the Docker installation runs Metacheck’s website on your own computer, with the same checks. It needs about 1.7 GB of disk space and a computer with 8 GB of memory, plus Docker. There, the code of a repository runs inside Metacheck’s own container: it cannot reach the files on your computer, but unlike in the sandbox described above, it can use the internet. The packages the code needs are downloaded while the check runs. Running the check on your own computer also means that an unpublished manuscript never leaves it, which matters for editors and reviewers who may not upload a submission to an external server.

The easiest way to try the check is our server on SURF Research Cloud, which runs on the servers of SURF, the cooperative of the Dutch universities, in the Netherlands. You need nothing but a web browser. On Metacheck’s website, upload a PDF under Run Metacheck on a Paper and tick Also run the code in the paper’s repository, or, under Run Metacheck on a Repository, choose a folder or a .zip file, or paste a link to an online repository such as GitHub or OSF. Uploaded files are deleted as soon as they have been read, and the report is kept on the server for one hour, so save it if you want to keep it.

The server’s capacity is shared by everyone who uses it, so it is meant for checking a paper or a repository now and then. If you want to check many papers, run Metacheck on your own computer, or build your own server on SURF Research Cloud, which researchers at Dutch institutions can do through their institution or with a free NWO grant. The Setting up Metacheck chapter describes all these options.

Running the reproducibility check in R.

I will illustrate the reproducibility check module in R. Metacheck reads a paper from its PDF. We download both PDFs from GitHub, and convert() turns each into a structured file that read() loads into R. If you want to follow along in the Metacheck website, download the two papers from here and here.

download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper/main/output/analysis.pdf",
  destfile = "good_paper.pdf", mode = "wb"
)
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/analysis.pdf",
  destfile = "bad_paper.pdf", mode = "wb"
)
paper <- read(convert(file_path = "good_paper.pdf", save_path = "."))
bad_paper <- read(convert(file_path = "bad_paper.pdf", save_path = "."))

Both papers link to their repository. The repo_check module in Metacheck supports over 270 data repositories, and can automatically download files from these repositories.

Running the module is a single line. By default, reproducibility_check only inspects the code without running it. execute = TRUE is needed to actually run the full computational reproducibility check:

mo_good <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check", execute = TRUE)
mo_good$traffic_light
#> [1] "green"
cat(mo_good$summary_text)
#> 
#> -  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated subprocess).
#> -  2 files appear runnable so far (parses, inputs resolve, placeable in the run order).
#> -  2 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
#> -  5 installable dependencies detected.
#> - 39 statistics stored from the extracted output; 11 of 11 reported tests matched (100%).

The light is green: every script ran without an error, and every result reported in the manuscript was among the results the code produced when it ran. mo_good$table lists each script and what happened when it was run:

mo_good$table[, c("file_name", "outcome")]
#>                 file_name outcome
#> analysis.qmd analysis.qmd  ran_ok
#> clean_data.R clean_data.R  ran_ok

clean_data.R turns the raw data file into the processed data file, and analysis.qmd is the manuscript, whose code chunks contain the analysis. The repository also contains renv/activate.R, a script the renv package adds to a project to set up its package library. The module does not check the contents of this folder, because it knows it is not part of the analysis.

mo_good$match_table shows, for each result reported in the paper, whether it was found in the output of the code, and in which analysis:

mo_good$match_table[, c("reported", "found", "confidence", "analysis")] |>
  knitr::kable()
reportedfoundconfidenceanalysis
M=15.1TRUEfullmean by group
M=23TRUEfullmean by group
SD=4.1TRUEfullsd by group
SD=4.78TRUEfullsd by group
r=0.37 t=4.53 df=129 p=<0.001TRUEfullPearson’s product-moment correlation
t=18.04 df=130 p=<0.001TRUEfullPaired t-test
Cohen’s dz=1.58TRUEfulld_z
M=7.77TRUEfullmean by group
M=8.13TRUEfullmean by group
t=-0.42 df=120.37 p=0.673TRUEfullWelch Two Sample t-test
Cohen’s d=-0.07TRUEfullCohens_d

A result is not compared as single numbers, but as a whole: the t-value, the degrees of freedom, and the p-value of one test have to appear together in the output of one analysis. Any single number will sooner or later turn up somewhere in a large output by coincidence, but several numbers of one test appearing together in one analysis will not.

Making your own results findable

The module can only find a result if the code produces it while it runs, in a form the module recognises. In the good paper, every reported number is computed in a code chunk, and the text of the manuscript only rounds these values. A number that is computed only inside the text, by an inline R expression in Quarto or R Markdown, is not part of the code that is run, so it cannot be found.

The module recognises the results of test functions such as t.test() and cor.test(), of summaries such as sapply(stroop_data[, c("congruent", "incongruent")], mean), and of effect sizes from the effectsize package, also when they are stored in a variable (ttest_result <- t.test(...)). A number computed by hand, such as a Cohen’s d computed as mean(diff) / sd(diff), is found when the code prints it, but not when it is only stored in a variable.

A green light means that the numbers in the paper follow from the shared code and data. It does not mean that the analysis was the right one to perform.

Now let’s see what the module returns if we run it on the bad paper:

mo_bad <- module_run(bad_paper, "reproducibility_check", execute = TRUE)
mo_bad$traffic_light
#> [1] "red"
cat(mo_bad$summary_text)
#> 
#> -  We assessed AND ran 1 R code file for reproducibility (each in an isolated subprocess).
#> -  1 file appears runnable so far (parses, inputs resolve, placeable in the run order).
#> -  0 of 1 script ran without error when executed.
#> -  3 installable dependencies detected.
#> - 10 statistics stored from the extracted output; 2 of 6 reported tests matched (33.3%).

The light is red, because the analysis code stopped with an error:

mo_bad$table[, c("file_name", "outcome")]
#>                 file_name outcome
#> analysis.qmd analysis.qmd errored
cat(mo_bad$run_results$error)
#> ! in callr subprocess.
#> Caused by error in `eval(predvars, data, env)`:
#> ! object 'stroop_effect' not found

The code compares the Stroop effect between the two years using a column stroop_effect, but no line of the code creates that column. The authors presumably created it in their R console while they worked, so the code ran on their own computer, but it cannot run for anyone else. This is one of the most common reasons shared code fails.

Before the code was run, the module also changed one line of it. mo_bad$modifications lists every change:

mods <- mo_bad$modifications
mods[mods$change_type == "setwd_removed", c("change_type", "detail")]
#>     change_type                                detail
#> 2 setwd_removed C:/Users/dlakens/Desktop/stroop_study

The code starts with setwd("C:/Users/dlakens/Desktop/stroop_study"), which sets the folder R works in to a folder that only exists on the author’s computer. The module skips this line, and reports that it did, because it would stop the code on any other computer.

Now the comparison between the paper and the output:

mo_bad$match_table[, c("reported", "found", "confidence", "analysis")] |>
  knitr::kable()
reportedfoundconfidenceanalysis
t=18.04 df=130 p=0.25 Cohen’s dz=0.25FALSEnoneNA
t=-0.42 df=120.37 p=0.673FALSEnoneNA
M=15.1TRUEfullmean by group
SD=4.1TRUEfullsd by group
M=23 SD=4.78FALSEnoneNA
r=0.37FALSEnoneNA

Only the mean and standard deviation of the congruent condition were found. Each of the other results is missing for a different reason:

  • The incongruent mean and standard deviation (M = 23.0, SD = 4.78) are not in the output. The output contains the statistics the code did compute:

    mo_bad$stat_output[[1]]$long[, c("analysis", "statistic", "value")]
    #>         analysis       statistic                value
#> 1  mean by group            mean     15.1102878787879
#> 2  mean by group            mean      22.080446969697
#> 3    sd by group              sd     4.08488216267072
#> 4    sd by group              sd       11.63934788467
#> 5  Paired t-test               t     6.77356838604279
#> 6  Paired t-test              df                  131
#> 7  Paired t-test               p 3.84360296105763e-10
#> 8  Paired t-test mean difference     6.97015909090909
#> 9  Paired t-test        conf.low     4.93450571703671
#> 10 Paired t-test       conf.high     9.00581246478147

    The incongruent mean is 22.08, with a standard deviation of 11.64. The reason is in the data. One participant has a reaction time of -99 in the incongruent condition:

    bad_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/stroop.csv")
summary(bad_data$Incongruent)
    #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  -99.00   19.27   22.64   22.08   26.10   35.13

    -99 is a code for a missing value, not a reaction time. The authors removed this participant before computing the results in their paper, but the code they shared does not, so it analyses -99 as if it were a reaction time.

  • The paired t-test, t(130) = 18.04, is not found for the same reason: the shared code analyses all 132 participants, including the -99, and gets t(131) = 6.77. The reported p = .25 and Cohen’s dz = 0.25 would not have matched in any case, because neither is consistent with a t-value of 18.04 (the StatCheck and Effect Sizes modules flag both from the text alone).

  • The correlation, r = 0.37, is reported, but no line of the code computes it.

  • The comparison between the years, t(120.37) = -0.42, p = .673, has exactly the numbers the good paper reports, so it is probably correct. But the code stopped with an error before it reached this test, so it cannot be verified from what the authors shared.

The three p-values about accuracy (p = .07, p = .34, and p = .000) are not in the table at all. The module only checks a p-value that is reported together with its test statistic. Had they been checked, they would not have been found either: the repository contains no accuracy data.

Open for feedback

Making this software was a challenge. We have validated the code by running it on more than 3000 scientific papers, with hundreds of folders of data and code, across dozens of data repositories. But there will be bugs. Software this complex, that tries to process the almost infinite ways in which researchers can share data and code, is bound to run into bugs. When thousands of people try this out, for some it will fail on their very first try (while for many others, it will run fine). If you find a bug, please raise an issue on the Metacheck github page. You need to share the data or code files that lead to the problem with us, or we can’t fix the problem. If you can’t share the data and code, you can ask an AI agent to analyze the problem, which might be enough to solve it as well. If the tool lacks features you would like to have, let us know, and we will do our best to build them in.

articles.title: Registration is now full for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp
articles.content:
The demand for the 2024 ERP Boot Camp was far beyond our expectations, and we reached our maximum registration of 30 people within one day. We already have a waiting list of over 30 people, so we have closed the registration site.

We realize that this is very disappointing to many people. We hope to offer another workshop like this next summer, or possibly earlier.

If you would like to get announcements about upcoming boot camps and webinars, you should join our email list.

You may also consider hosting a Mini ERP Boot Camp at your institution (in person or over Zoom).

articles.title: New Paper: Using Multivariate Pattern Analysis to Increase Effect Sizes for ERP Amplitude Comparisons
articles.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Bahle, B., Simmons, A. M., & Luck, S. J. (2024). Using multivariate pattern analysis to increase effect sizes for event-related potential analyses. Psychophysiology, 61, e14570. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14570 [preprint]

Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) can be used to “decode” subtle information from ERP signals, such as which of several faces a participant is perceiving or the orientation that someone is holding in working memory (see this previous blog post). This approach is so powerful that we started wondering whether it might also give us greater statistical power in more typical experiments where the goal is to determine whether an ERP component differs in amplitude across experimental conditions. For example, might we more easily be able to tell if N400 amplitude is different between two different classes of words by using decoding? If so, that might make it possible to detect effects that would otherwise be too small to be significant.

To address this question, we compared decoding with the conventional ERP analysis approach with using the 6 experimental paradigms in the ERP CORE. In the conventional ERP analysis, we measured the mean amplitude during the standard measurement window from each participant in the two conditions of the paradigm (e.g., faces versus cars for N170, deviants versus standards for MMN). We quantified the magnitude of the difference between conditions using Cohen’s dz (the variant of Cohen’s d corresponding to a paired t test). For example, the effect size in the conventional ERP comparison of faces versus cars in the N170 paradigm was approximately 1.7 (see the figure).

We also applied decoding to each paradigm. For example, in the N170 paradigm, we trained a support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish between ERPs elicited by faces and ERPs elicited by cars. This was done separately for each subject, and we converted the decoding accuracy into Cohen’s dz so that it could be compared with the dz from the conventional ERP analysis. As you can see from the bar labeled SVM in the figure above, the effect size for the SVM-based decoding analysis was almost twice as large as the effect size for the conventional ERP analysis. That’s a huge difference!

We found a similar benefit for SVM-based decoding over conventional ERP analyses in 7 of the 10 cases we tested (see the figure below). In the other 3 cases, the ERP and SVM effects were approximately equivalent. So, there doesn’t seem to be a downside to using decoding, at least in terms of effect size. But there can be a big benefit.

Because decoding has many possible benefits, we’ve added it into ERPLAB Toolbox. It’s super easy to use, and we’ve created detailed documentation and a video to explain how it works at a conceptual level and to show you how to use it.

We encourage you to apply it to your own data. It may give you the power to detect effects that are too small to be detected with conventional ERP analyses.

articles.title: Phenotypic screening in Parkinson's iPSC-dopamine neurons identifies the FASN-SREBP1 axis as a potential therapeutic target
articles.content: Parkinson's disease (PD) remains highly challenging to model in vitro, particularly when seeking robust functional phenotypes for target discovery. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell dopaminergic neurons (iPSC-DANs) offer a promising platform to address this challenge. Because calcium dyshomeostasis is well-described in PD pathophysiology, it offers a platform for phenotypic screening. We have previously shown that GBA-N370S iPSC-DANs display impaired intracellular calcium release. Here, we used this disease-relevant phenotype to undertake a 4,108-compound phenotypic screen in GBA-N370S (GBA-NS) iPSC-DANs. This screen identified fatty acid synthase (FASN) as the most enriched protein target. The ability of compounds to rescue calcium release correlated with biochemical potency against FASN across multiple chemical series. We confirmed that FASN knockdown increased intracellular calcium release, supporting an on-target effect. Untargeted lipidomics demonstrated broad remodelling of the neuronal lipidome after FASN inhibition, confirming target engagement. FASN inhibition also increased active a-glucocerebrosidase (GCase), reduced extracellular a-synuclein release and ER stress, and altered RASGRF1 expression. Mechanistically, FASN inhibition activated sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), and SREBP1 overexpression alone was sufficient to increase intracellular calcium release, identifying a FASN-SREBP1-calcium homeostasis axis in human neurons. Finally, the FASN inhibitor BI 99179 achieved brain exposure and reduced brain fatty acid levels while inducing an SRE-associated transcriptional response in a Parkinson's mouse model, providing evidence of in vivo target engagement. These findings establish patient iPSC-neuron functional screening as a tractable discovery platform to identify targets which can be taken in vivo and nominate the FASN-SREBP1 axis as a candidate therapeutic pathway in PD.

articles.title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction
articles.content: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures—cells, neurons and vasculature—and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains—from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification—into a single, accessible software environment.
articles.author: Tingwei Quan

articles.title: Natural language processing for suicidal behavior detection in short Spanish clinical notes from first-contact interviews
articles.content: IntroductionSuicide is a multifactorial phenomenon influenced by social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors, whose early detection remains challenging. According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 years, representing a major public health concern for young populations worldwide. In first-contact clinical settings, screening opportunities are often constrained by limited time, sparse patient information, and operational workflows. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting suicidal behavior from short Spanish-language texts collected during initial screening interviews.MethodsThe dataset comprises 374 anonymized records labeled as “no suicidal behavior,” “ideation,” “planning,” or “attempt,” with a strong imbalance toward “attempt,” reflecting operational clinical usage rather than population-representative sampling. To address data scarcity, we applied data augmentation methods (Easy Data Augmentation for Spanish, backtranslation, and large language model-based synthesis), validated through statistical analysis and clinician-based plausibility assessments.ResultsExploratory analyses revealed highly constrained and overlapping lexical patterns across classes, indicating the challenging nature of the task. A Support Vector Machine achieved 0.53 macro F1 in binary classification (“suicidal behavior” vs. “no behavior”), while BETO, a Spanish BERT model, reached 0.36 macro F1 in multiclass classification. Under the same text-only conditions, human specialists achieved macro F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.15 respectively; however, these results were based on only 20 real texts evaluated with double annotation across five specialists and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.DiscussionAlthough performance is modest compared to studies using full clinical records, these findings suggest that short-text machine learning could support nonspecialists in first-contact settings. Future work should expand datasets and explore multimodal approaches, including voice and text, to improve clinical applicability and early detection.
articles.author: Ansel Y. Rodríguez-González

articles.title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models
articles.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.
articles.author: Bocheng Wang

articles.title: Mechanonociceptive tactile feedback enhances prosthetic grasp control during repeated human-in-the-loop interaction
articles.content: Upper-limb prosthetic systems continue to face a fundamental challenge in providing sensory feedback that remains functionally effective during repeated interaction. This study investigates innocuous painful feedback (IPF), a controlled mechanonociceptive tactile modality intended to provide salient error-related information during human-in-the-loop prosthetic interaction. A custom experimental platform was developed to emulate prosthetic grasping conditions in healthy participants, enabling systematic evaluation of IPF across feedback modality, stimulation frequency, temporal modulation strategy, and spatial configuration. IPF was associated with lower grasp-position errors than visual-only and visual-plus-force feedback, supporting its potential as a corrective sensory feedback modality for boundary-constrained grasp control. Within the tested frequency range, high-frequency stimulation produced the lowest error levels, demonstrating that the functional effectiveness of IPF depends on stimulation frequency. Progressive frequency modulation generally maintained lower error levels than fixed-frequency stimulation across repeated interaction, while sequential dual-site stimulation yielded lower overall participant-level errors than repeated single-site stimulation, although the magnitude of this difference varied across the trial sequence. Collectively, these findings indicate that the behavioral effectiveness of mechanonociceptive feedback depends not only on feedback modality, but also on its temporal and spatial organization. As a proof-of-concept study conducted in neurologically intact participants using a virtual prosthetic-like grasping paradigm, these findings provide a basis for subsequent validation with individuals with upper-limb amputation and physical prosthetic devices.
articles.author: Elif Hocaoglu

articles.title: Brain-inspired predictive visual attention for spatiotemporal semantic understanding of complex film and television videos
articles.content: Due to the unique characteristics of film and television, such as montage editing and narrative structure jumps, semantically salient targets frequently experience temporal feature drift, making it difficult for existing models to maintain stable semantic understanding output when keyframes are lost. Inspired by predictive coding mechanisms in neuroscience, this paper proposes a spatiotemporal joint representation framework driven by brain-like visual attention. A pixel-level saliency heatmap is constructed using eye-tracking data as a physiological-level supervisory signal. A Dual-Stream Spatio-Temporal Encoding Network (DS-STEN) is designed: the spatial stream uses ResNet to extract single-frame salient features, while the temporal stream uses 3D convolution to model the optical flow field and capture cross-frame trajectories. A Kalman filter-driven predictive attention module is introduced into the fusion layer to estimate the target’s position and feature distribution in the next frame. The prediction results are injected into the temporal stream as a priori mask to actively correct abnormal responses during drift. The corrected spatiotemporal features are aggregated with semantic context through a Transformer cross-frame self-attention layer and input into a semantic classification head to generate scene-level and event-level labels. End-to-end joint training is performed using a weighted loss of saliency prediction, trajectory consistency, and semantic classification. Experiments show that the saliency prediction correlation coefficient (CC) reaches 0.846 and the normalized scanpath saliency (NSS) reaches 2.47 on the AIM2024 benchmark. In the TVQA+ dataset target tracking task, the cross-frame tracking accuracy in unoccluded scenes reaches 95.3%. In the MovieNet dataset scene semantic classification task, the average accuracy for Dialogue scenes reaches 93.5%. This paper provides a new spatiotemporal modeling paradigm with a neuroscience basis for semantic understanding of complex film and television videos.
articles.author: Peng Han

articles.title: MS-3D-CNN with quantum-inspired chaotic hybrid adaptive wolf-particle swarm optimization for tactical pattern classification in basketball from player tracking data
articles.content: IntroductionAI sport analysis methods have been considerably improved by developments in knowledge of tactically information and its codification. Nevertheless, methods for capturing multi-levels spatio-temporal information for complex team-sport behaviors are still limited. In opposed to motion recognition, which concentrates on movements of individual athlete, tactically pattern classification refers to the recognition of coordinated group actions based mostly on the athlete space-time trajectories.MethodsAn efficient Q16 framework based on MS-3D-CNN and Chaotic Opposition-based Adaptive Wolf-Particle Swarm Optimization (QIC-HAWPSO) for action recognition is proposed in this paper. Parallel multi-scale 3D kernels (three different scales of 3, 5, and 7 frames which correspond to 0.12, 0.20, and 0.28 seconds) are used to learn quick individual actions, complex actions, as well as slow formations. QIC-HAWPSO has chaos opposition-based learning, quantum tunneling adaptive mechanism, and population diversity awareness.ResultsThe framework demonstrated an accuracy of 94.3% on the Basketball-51 dataset (10,311 clips for 8 types of tactical action), leading the current 7 state-of-the-art approaches, such as Game Sense (92.8%), ACA-Net (89.3%), and HAWPSO-3D-CNN (90.1%). Moreover, the inference latency can be evaluated at 34.2 ms clip-1 based on precomputed tracking-grid input and a memory size of 2.4 GB.DiscussionThe classifier will be useful in online coaching, broadcasting, and player analysis, depending on upstream tracking data. It consists of a multi-scale MS-3D-CNN framework, a superior QIC-HAWPSO optimizer, and experimental results that demonstrate the importance of the approach over baseline strategies.
articles.author: Haoyan Liu

articles.title: Cross-subject EEG driving fatigue detection: early personal spectral reference and causal long-sequence residual encoding
articles.content: BackgroundIn cross-subject electroencephalography (EEG)-based driving-fatigue detection, most existing decoders are designed around second-scale short windows, whereas fatigue is a slow drift; short-window spectral features provide little direct evidence of that slow drift, limiting fatigue decisions. More critically, each individual’s spectral baseline level and fatigue-change pattern differ, so simply lengthening the window still leaves models struggling to predict across individuals from observed spectral features. This work aims to enable cross-subject fatigue decisions under shared parameters, without per-driver specialized models.MethodsWe propose early personal spectral reference with causal long-sequence residual encoding: an early personal spectral reference is estimated only from a short session-opening spectral window; subsequent spectral observations are mapped into residual space; state-conditioned temporal modeling accumulates and updates a residual state over a long causal sequence; and fatigue is read out from the terminal state.ResultsOn leave-one-subject-out binary classification of the Multimodal Phenotyping Dataset of Driving Fatigue (MPD-DF), five-seed (2026–2030) macro-averaged F1 is 0.655 ± 0.005 (0.660 at seed 2026), outperforming the best matched-protocol absolute-spectrum baseline (≈0.587). On continuous vigilance regression of the SEED Vigilance dataset (SEED-VIG) under a subject-LOSO protocol, root mean square error (RMSE) is 0.209 ± 0.005 under 5Bands and 0.200 ± 0.003 under 2 Hz, both below matched-protocol baselines.ConclusionAn early personal spectrum estimated from a short opening window can reduce interference from intrinsic individual spectral level in fatigue decisions and provides a practical premise for cross-subject fatigue decoding. Accumulating and updating residual state over a causal long sequence in residual space further improves cross-subject decisions. Under shared parameters without per-driver models, the framework outperforms matched absolute-spectrum baselines on both fatigue classification and vigilance regression.
articles.author: Lanlan Lv

articles.title: A progenitor with immature Bergmann glia-like characteristics in the developing cerebellar cortex
articles.content: The cerebellum is an ancient brain component, conserved across mammalian species, that has classically played roles in regulating muscle tone, limb coordination, and equilibrium, as well as in non-motor functions, such as language, cognition, and emotion. Recently, we reported Nestin-expressing cells in the cerebellar cortex of ferret neonates that showed a proliferative potency defined by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) immunostaining. We called these cells “internal granular progenitor (IGP).” IGPs were found to be abundant in the internal granular layer adjacent to the Purkinje cell layer and extended GFAP-immunopositive radials progressed through the molecular and external granular layers, forming an immature Bergmann glia-like morphology. The tracking of BrdU-labeling revealed that IGPs differentiated into granular neurons, Bergmann glia, and/or astrocytes. As such, we propose that IGPs may be neural progenitors with an immature Bergmann glia-like morphology that appear in the developing cerebellar cortex, and could serve as another source of granular neurons distinct from external granular progenitors. Further research on IGPs is expected to provide new perspectives for the future investigation of cerebellar corticohistogensis, particularly the difference between motor and non-motor cerebellar regions, and how the abnormal development of IGPs relates to neurodevelopmental disorders associated with non-motor cerebellar function, such as autism spectrum disorder.
articles.author: Kazuhiko Sawada

articles.title: Cerebral blood flow asymmetry in motor-related regions is associated with 30-day upper-limb motor recovery after acute ischemic stroke
articles.content: BackgroundUpper-limb motor impairment is a leading cause of long-term disability after acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet early prognostication relies mainly on clinical scales. Cerebral blood flow (CBF) asymmetry measured by arterial spin labeling (ASL) perfusion MRI may indicate recovery potential. We investigated whether acute-phase CBF asymmetry indices (AIs) in six motor-related regions are associated with 30-day upper-limb motor recovery.MethodsSixty patients with AIS underwent pseudo-continuous ASL MRI within 72 h of onset and completed the 30-day Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Upper Extremity (FMA-UE). Patients were classified into good (n = 30, ΔFMA-UE ≥ 10) and poor (n = 30, ΔFMA-UE ≤ 4) recovery groups; both thresholds lie outside the published minimal clinically important difference range, and no patient fell between them. Mean CBF was extracted bilaterally from the precentral and postcentral gyri, supplementary motor area, putamen, pallidum, and thalamus, and AIs were calculated. Regional AI–ΔFMA-UE associations were assessed with Spearman correlation, partial correlation, analysis of covariance, and linear regression.ResultsPrecentral and postcentral gyrus AIs each correlated positively with ΔFMA-UE (both Spearman r = 0.30, p = 0.020; false-discovery-rate q = 0.020), persisting after adjustment for cognitive status, baseline FMA-UE, and lesion volume (partial r up to 0.326; all p < 0.05); other regional AIs showed negligible correlations (|r| < 0.09). In analysis of covariance (follow-up FMA-UE as outcome, baseline FMA-UE as covariate), precentral gyrus AI remained associated with the outcome (β = 0.13, 95% CI 0.01–0.25, p = 0.037; after cognitive adjustment, p = 0.045). A model combining the six AIs with age and cognitive status explained 29.7% of variance in ΔFMA-UE (F(8,51) = 2.69, p = 0.015), but adding the AIs to clinical variables alone did not significantly improve explanatory performance (ΔR2 = 0.048, p = 0.170); this R2 reflects the combined imaging–clinical model rather than ASL alone.ConclusionSensorimotor-cortex CBF asymmetry within 72 h of onset was associated with 30-day upper-limb motor recovery after AIS, robust to adjustment for clinical variables. Acute-phase ASL may serve as a noninvasive imaging indicator for recovery-oriented rehabilitation stratification, a hypothesis requiring further validation.
